passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A research team isolates a small globular protein, which they call vantagin, from pancreatic tissue. The mature protein is a single chain of 128 amino acids that folds into a compact shape with most of its nonpolar side chains buried in the interior. Three pairs of cysteine residues form disulfide bonds that lock the folded shape in place.

To probe how structure supports function, the team measures the protein's net charge across a pH gradient and finds it carries no net charge at pH 6.8. Separately, they treat active protein with heat, with a reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds, and with a detergent that disrupts noncovalent contacts. Each treatment abolishes activity, yet analysis shows the peptide backbone remains intact.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 3 (Biological Macromolecules)

questions.stem: The team loads vantagin onto a column buffered at pH 4.0. Based on its behavior in the pH gradient, what net charge will the protein most likely carry?
choices: Net positive, because the pH is below its isoelectric point
Net negative, because the pH is below its isoelectric point
No net charge, because pH 4.0 equals its isoelectric point
No charge at all, because the buried residues are nonpolar
questions.explain: At a pH below the isoelectric point of 6.8, acidic and basic groups gain protons, so the protein carries a net positive charge.

questions.stem: The reducing agent abolishes activity even though the amino acid sequence is unchanged. What does this best demonstrate about the disulfide bonds?
choices: They form part of the primary sequence that encodes the protein
They stabilize the folded three dimensional shape needed for activity
They are the peptide bonds that link adjacent residues
They shield the protein from changes in solution pH
questions.explain: Disulfide bonds are covalent cross links that stabilize tertiary structure, so breaking them lets the chain unfold and lose function even though the sequence is intact.

questions.stem: Heating the solution destroys activity but leaves every peptide bond intact. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Heat changed the order of amino acids in the chain
Heat added new amino acids to the active site
Heat disrupted higher order folding while the primary structure was preserved
Heat converted the protein into a different polymer
questions.explain: Denaturation disrupts the noncovalent interactions that hold secondary and tertiary structure, so the protein unfolds and loses function while its covalent sequence stays the same.

questions.stem: Why are most nonpolar side chains found buried in the protein's interior rather than on its surface?
choices: Nonpolar groups form strong hydrogen bonds with surrounding water
Nonpolar groups carry negative charges that repel one another
Only nonpolar groups can form peptide bonds
Burying nonpolar groups away from water is favorable in an aqueous cell
questions.explain: In water, clustering hydrophobic side chains in the interior minimizes their contact with water and helps drive folding.

questions.stem: A later study shows the active enzyme is actually two identical vantagin chains bound together. A single substitution at the contact surface blocks the two chains from associating without changing how either chain folds on its own. The lost activity is best explained by disruption of which structural level?
choices: Quaternary structure
Primary structure
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
questions.explain: Quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple folded subunits, so preventing the subunits from associating removes quaternary structure while each chain's own fold is unchanged.

questions.stem: Spectroscopy reveals a repeating pattern of hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and backbone amide hydrogens, producing regular coils and sheets. These features are examples of which level of protein structure?
choices: Primary structure
Secondary structure
Tertiary structure
Quaternary structure
questions.explain: Regular local folding such as alpha helices and beta sheets, stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds, defines secondary structure.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A different team studies an enzyme, hydrolase X, that cleaves a colorless substrate into a colored product, letting them track reaction rate by color intensity. They hold the amount of enzyme fixed and vary substrate concentration, recording the initial rate at each level.

As substrate rises, the rate climbs steeply at first and then levels off at a maximum, Vmax. The team then repeats the experiment with two candidate drugs. Drug A raises the substrate concentration needed to reach half of Vmax but does not change Vmax. Drug B lowers Vmax while leaving the half maximal substrate concentration unchanged.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 6 (Metabolism)

questions.stem: Why does the reaction rate level off at high substrate concentration?
choices: The substrate begins to inhibit itself at high levels
The product is being converted back into substrate
Nearly all enzyme active sites are occupied, so the enzyme is saturated
The enzyme is permanently denatured by excess substrate
questions.explain: At saturating substrate, essentially all active sites are occupied at any instant, so adding more substrate cannot raise the rate and the enzyme works at its maximum.

questions.stem: Drug A increases the substrate concentration needed to reach half of Vmax but does not change Vmax. This pattern is most consistent with which type of inhibition?
choices: Noncompetitive inhibition
Irreversible denaturation
Feedback activation
Competitive inhibition
questions.explain: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half maximal rate, yet enough substrate can still drive the reaction to the normal Vmax.

questions.stem: Drug B lowers Vmax while leaving the half maximal substrate concentration unchanged, and adding more substrate does not restore the original maximum rate. Which mechanism best explains Drug B?
choices: It binds a site other than the active site and reduces the number of functional enzymes
It binds the active site and competes with substrate
It increases the enzyme's affinity for substrate
It is consumed as a second substrate
questions.explain: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site and lowers Vmax, and because it does not compete for the active site, extra substrate cannot overcome it and the half maximal point is unchanged.

questions.stem: For the enzyme exposed to Drug A, what should happen to the reaction rate if the team greatly increases substrate concentration?
choices: The rate stays suppressed no matter how much substrate is added
The rate can approach the original Vmax as substrate outcompetes the drug
Vmax will rise above the drug free value
The enzyme will switch to making a different product
questions.explain: Because a competitive inhibitor and substrate compete for the same site, high substrate concentration outcompetes the inhibitor and the rate approaches the normal Vmax.

questions.stem: The team finds hydrolase X works best near 37 C and loses almost all activity at 70 C, with activity that does not return on cooling. What is the most likely reason for the loss at 70 C?
choices: The substrate evaporated at 70 C
The enzyme ran out of active sites
The high temperature permanently denatured the enzyme
High temperature made the reaction thermodynamically impossible
questions.explain: Well above its optimum, heat disrupts the folded active site, and because the shape does not refold on cooling, activity does not return.

questions.stem: In the cell, the end product of hydrolase X's pathway binds a distant regulatory site on the enzyme and slows it down, so flux through the pathway drops when product accumulates. This regulation is best described as...
choices: Competitive inhibition at the active site
An increase in Vmax caused by the product
Irreversible covalent modification of the substrate
Allosteric feedback inhibition
questions.explain: Binding of the pathway's end product to a separate regulatory site that reduces activity is allosteric feedback inhibition, a common way cells match output to demand.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A lab engineers a bacterial strain to study how a single gene is expressed into a functional protein. They can label newly made RNA and newly made protein separately, and they can introduce precise changes into the gene's DNA sequence.

In one experiment they insert a single extra nucleotide near the start of the protein coding region. In another they change a single base so that a codon that once specified an amino acid becomes a stop codon. They then compare the length and activity of the protein produced in each case.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 15 (Genes and Proteins)

questions.stem: Inserting a single extra nucleotide near the start of the coding region abolishes the protein's function almost completely. What is the best explanation?
choices: The insertion shifts the reading frame, so most codons downstream are misread
The insertion only changes one amino acid and leaves the rest normal
Extra nucleotides cannot be transcribed into RNA
The ribosome simply skips the extra nucleotide
questions.explain: Because codons are read in nonoverlapping groups of three, adding one nucleotide shifts the reading frame and changes essentially every downstream codon, usually destroying function.

questions.stem: Changing one base converts an internal codon into a stop codon. Compared with normal protein, the product of this gene will most likely be...
choices: Longer than normal because translation continues past the change
Truncated because translation stops early
The same length but with one different amino acid
Unchanged because stop codons are ignored inside a gene
questions.explain: A premature stop codon ends translation early, producing a shortened protein that is usually nonfunctional.

questions.stem: A third change swaps one base but the encoded amino acid stays the same, and the protein is fully active. This outcome is best explained by which feature of the genetic code?
choices: The code is read one base at a time
tRNA can carry any amino acid to any codon
The code is degenerate, so several codons can specify the same amino acid
The ribosome proofreads and corrects the base
questions.explain: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, so some single base changes are silent and do not alter the protein.

questions.stem: The team labels newly made RNA and finds label appears in RNA before any labeled protein shows up. Which ordering of events does this support?
choices: Protein is made first and then copied into RNA
RNA and protein are made independently of the gene
Protein is translated directly from DNA without RNA
DNA is transcribed into RNA, which is then translated into protein
questions.explain: RNA is synthesized from the DNA template during transcription and then serves as the message for protein synthesis during translation, so labeled RNA precedes labeled protein.

questions.stem: Which cellular machine directly reads the messenger RNA codons and joins amino acids into a chain?
choices: The ribosome
RNA polymerase
DNA polymerase
The spliceosome
questions.explain: The ribosome binds mRNA, pairs each codon with the matching aminoacyl tRNA, and catalyzes peptide bond formation during translation.

questions.stem: The bacterium normally makes this protein only when a specific sugar is present. When the sugar is absent, a repressor binds the DNA and blocks transcription, and adding the sugar relieves the block. This behavior is characteristic of...
choices: A constitutive gene that is always on
An inducible operon controlled by a repressor
A gene lacking any promoter
A eukaryotic enhancer far from the gene
questions.explain: An inducible operon is normally off because a repressor blocks transcription, and the inducer, here the sugar, inactivates the repressor so transcription can proceed, matching the lac operon logic.

passages.label: Cross
paragraphs: A plant breeder studies flower color and stem height in a garden species. Flower color shows two forms, purple and white, and stem height shows tall and short. From earlier crosses the breeder knows that purple is dominant to white and tall is dominant to short, and the two genes sit on different chromosomes.

The breeder crosses a plant that is heterozygous for both traits with a plant that is white flowered and short. Hundreds of offspring are scored for both traits, and the breeder also tracks how alleles are distributed into gametes.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 12 (Mendel's Experiments and Heredity)

questions.stem: The cross is a purple tall double heterozygote by a white short plant. Among the offspring, what phenotype ratio is expected for the four combinations?
choices: 9 purple tall : 3 purple short : 3 white tall : 1 white short
3 purple tall : 1 white short
1 purple tall : 1 purple short : 1 white tall : 1 white short
All offspring purple and tall
questions.explain: A test cross of a double heterozygote to a fully recessive parent gives a 1 to 1 to 1 to 1 ratio of the four phenotype combinations.

questions.stem: The equal 1 to 1 to 1 to 1 result, with new trait combinations appearing, is best explained by which principle?
choices: The two genes are tightly linked and inherited together
One trait blends into the other in offspring
Both traits are controlled by a single gene
Genes on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis
questions.explain: Because the two genes are on different chromosomes, they assort independently in meiosis, producing all four gamete types in equal proportions.

questions.stem: A white flowered plant always breeds true for white when self crossed. What does this indicate about the white allele?
choices: White is the recessive phenotype, so white plants are homozygous recessive
White is dominant to purple
White plants must be heterozygous
White results from a new mutation in each plant
questions.explain: Because purple is dominant, a white plant must carry two recessive alleles, and homozygous recessive plants breed true for the recessive trait.

questions.stem: In a related species, two genes sit close together on the same chromosome. Compared with genes on different chromosomes, the alleles of these two linked genes will...
choices: Assort completely independently
Tend to be inherited together, with new combinations arising mainly through crossing over
Never recombine under any circumstances
Always produce a 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 ratio
questions.explain: Linked genes tend to travel together, and recombination between them occurs mainly by crossing over, so the closer they are, the rarer new combinations become.

questions.stem: In a large, randomly mating population at equilibrium, the recessive white phenotype appears in 16 percent of plants. What fraction of plants are expected to be heterozygous carriers?
questions.explain: If the recessive homozygote frequency is 0.16 then the recessive allele frequency is 0.4 and the dominant is 0.6, so heterozygotes equal two times 0.6 times 0.4, which is 0.48.

questions.stem: A fungus arrives that kills short plants before they reproduce but spares tall plants. Over several generations, what is the most likely effect on the allele for tall stems?
choices: Its frequency will fall because tall is dominant
It will stay exactly the same because mutation is random
The tall allele will disappear entirely in one generation
Its frequency will rise because tall plants leave more offspring
questions.explain: Selection that lets tall plants reproduce more raises the frequency of the tall allele over generations, the core idea of natural selection acting on heritable variation.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A physiology class studies how muscle cells generate ATP from glucose. They can measure oxygen use, glucose consumption, and the buildup of small molecules such as pyruvate and lactate in cultured cells under different oxygen conditions.

In one run, cells have plenty of oxygen. In another, oxygen is nearly removed. The class also uses a chemical that makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons, and they record what happens to ATP production and oxygen use.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 7 (Cellular Respiration)

questions.stem: When oxygen is nearly absent, the cells still make a small amount of ATP and accumulate lactate. Which pathway is supplying this ATP?
choices: Glycolysis followed by fermentation in the cytoplasm
Oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria
The citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix
Beta oxidation of fatty acids
questions.explain: Without oxygen, glycolysis in the cytoplasm still yields a net of two ATP per glucose, and fermentation to lactate regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

questions.stem: Why is converting pyruvate to lactate useful for a cell that has no oxygen?
choices: It produces most of the cell's ATP directly
It regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running
It stores oxygen for later use
It converts lactate into glucose for energy
questions.explain: Lactate fermentation reoxidizes NADH back to NAD+, the electron acceptor glycolysis needs, so without it glycolysis would stall once NAD+ ran out.

questions.stem: With oxygen present, the cells consume far more oxygen and make much more ATP per glucose. What direct role does oxygen play?
choices: It is the starting fuel that is split to release energy
It donates electrons to start the chain
It is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain
It is a product of the citric acid cycle
questions.explain: In aerobic respiration oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor of the electron transport chain, forming water, and without it the chain backs up and ATP output drops.

questions.stem: The chemical that makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons causes oxygen use to stay high while ATP production collapses. What best explains this result?
choices: The electron transport chain stops moving electrons
Oxygen can no longer accept electrons
Glycolysis is directly blocked by the chemical
The proton gradient is dissipated, so ATP synthase can no longer use it to make ATP
questions.explain: Uncouplers let protons leak back across the membrane, collapsing the gradient that drives ATP synthase, so electron transport and oxygen use continue but are no longer coupled to ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what the citric acid cycle contributes to ATP production?
choices: It produces electron carriers, NADH and FADH2, that feed the electron transport chain
It directly makes most of the cell's ATP
It consumes oxygen directly to make water
It converts glucose into pyruvate
questions.explain: The citric acid cycle harvests high energy electrons as NADH and FADH2, which then drive the electron transport chain where most ATP is made.

questions.stem: Cells use the energy released by breaking down glucose to attach a phosphate to ADP, forming ATP. Coupling an energy releasing reaction to an energy requiring one in this way means the overall process is...
choices: Impossible without an outside enzyme adding energy
Energetically favorable overall, releasing net free energy
Always exactly at equilibrium
Independent of the cell's energy needs
questions.explain: Cells couple exergonic reactions such as glucose breakdown to endergonic ones such as ATP synthesis so the combined process has a negative free energy change and proceeds.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: Students place animal cells that normally sit in a balanced salt solution into three beakers. Beaker 1 holds pure distilled water, beaker 2 holds a solution matched to the inside of the cell, and beaker 3 holds a concentrated salt solution far saltier than the cell interior.
They watch the cells under a microscope over several minutes and also track the activity of a membrane pump that uses ATP to move sodium out of the cell and potassium in against their gradients.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 5 (Structure and Function of Plasma Membranes)

questions.stem: In beaker 1, holding distilled water, what will most likely happen to the animal cells?
choices: They will shrink as water leaves
They will stay the same size
They will swell and may burst as water enters
They will actively pump water outward and stay unchanged
questions.explain: Distilled water is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves in by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration inside, swelling and possibly bursting the cell.

questions.stem: In beaker 3, holding concentrated salt, what is the expected change in the cells?
choices: They swell as salt enters
They stay the same size
They gain salt until they burst
They shrink as water leaves toward the saltier solution
questions.explain: The outside is hypertonic, so water leaves the cell by osmosis toward the higher external solute concentration and the cell shrinks.

questions.stem: The sodium potassium pump moves both ions against their concentration gradients and requires ATP. This is an example of...
choices: Primary active transport
Simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion
Osmosis
questions.explain: Moving ions against their gradients using energy taken directly from ATP is primary active transport.

questions.stem: A poison blocks ATP production in these cells. What is the most likely effect on the sodium potassium pump and the ion gradients?
choices: The pump speeds up to compensate
The pump stops and the sodium and potassium gradients gradually run down
The gradients grow stronger without ATP
Sodium is still pumped out but potassium stops moving
questions.explain: The pump depends on ATP, so without it pumping stops and ions leak down their gradients, dissipating the concentration differences over time.

questions.stem: The cells that keep their pumps running longest are those richest in mitochondria. Why would that be expected?
choices: Mitochondria store sodium for the pump
Mitochondria are where osmosis occurs
Mitochondria supply the ATP the pump needs
Mitochondria pump ions directly across the plasma membrane
questions.explain: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's ATP, so cells rich in mitochondria can sustain ATP dependent pumping longer.

questions.stem: A small nonpolar gas crosses the plasma membrane freely, but a charged ion cannot cross without a protein channel. Which membrane feature best explains this difference?
choices: The membrane is a single layer of protein
The membrane contains no proteins at all
Charged ions are too small to interact with the membrane
The hydrophobic interior of the lipid bilayer blocks charged particles but allows small nonpolar molecules
questions.explain: The nonpolar core of the phospholipid bilayer lets small uncharged nonpolar molecules pass but repels charged ions, which need transport proteins.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A microbiology team grows a bacterial culture and tracks its numbers over time. In fresh medium the population doubles at a steady interval, then slows as nutrients run low. The team also exposes the culture to an antibiotic and to a bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria.

They find that a few bacteria carry a small circular DNA molecule separate from the main chromosome that lets them survive the antibiotic. These survivors can pass copies of this molecule to neighboring bacteria through direct contact. Meanwhile, the bacteriophage injects its genetic material and forces the host to build new virus particles.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 21 (Viruses) and Ch. 22 (Prokaryotes: Bacteria and Archaea)

questions.stem: During the steady doubling phase, the number of bacteria over time increases...
choices: Exponentially, doubling each interval
Linearly, by the same number added each interval
By a decreasing amount each interval
Not at all until nutrients run out
questions.explain: Binary fission with a constant doubling time produces exponential growth, so the count multiplies rather than adding a fixed amount each interval.

questions.stem: The small circular DNA molecule that carries antibiotic survival and exists apart from the chromosome is best identified as a...
choices: Ribosome
Plasmid
Capsid
Nucleus
questions.explain: A plasmid is a small circular DNA molecule separate from the bacterial chromosome that often carries extra genes such as antibiotic resistance.

questions.stem: Survivors transfer copies of this resistance molecule to neighboring bacteria through direct contact. This form of horizontal gene transfer is...
choices: Binary fission
Mutation
Conjugation
Translation
questions.explain: Transfer of DNA, often a plasmid, between bacteria through direct cell to cell contact is conjugation, a route by which resistance spreads.

questions.stem: After antibiotic treatment, the surviving population is almost entirely resistant. What best explains this shift?
choices: The antibiotic taught the bacteria to resist it
Every bacterium mutated in response to the antibiotic
The antibiotic converted itself into food for the bacteria
The antibiotic killed susceptible cells and left resistant ones to reproduce
questions.explain: The antibiotic selects against susceptible cells, so pre existing resistant cells survive and reproduce and the population becomes dominated by resistant bacteria.

questions.stem: The bacteriophage must inject its genes and use the host's machinery to reproduce. This illustrates that viruses are...
choices: Obligate intracellular agents that require a host cell to replicate
Free living cells that grow by binary fission
Bacteria with an extra membrane
Organelles found inside bacteria
questions.explain: Viruses lack their own machinery to make proteins and energy, so they must hijack a host cell to replicate, making them obligate intracellular parasites.

questions.stem: In this infection the phage quickly forces the host to make many new virus particles that burst the cell to spread. This describes which viral pathway?
choices: The lysogenic cycle with a dormant integrated genome
The lytic cycle
Binary fission
Conjugation
questions.explain: Rapid production of new virions followed by lysis of the host cell is the lytic cycle, in contrast to the lysogenic cycle where the viral genome integrates and stays dormant.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A cancer biology lab studies how cells decide whether to divide. They grow cells in a dish and can measure DNA content per cell, detect damaged DNA, and switch specific regulatory proteins on or off. Normal cells pause at checkpoints if conditions are not right.

In one line, a checkpoint protein that normally halts the cycle when DNA is damaged has been inactivated. The team compares how normal cells and mutant cells respond after their DNA is damaged, and they also follow how a single fertilized egg gives rise to specialized tissues.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 10 (Cell Reproduction)

questions.stem: Before a normal cell divides, its measured DNA content doubles during one part of interphase. During which phase does this DNA doubling occur?
choices: G1 phase
M phase, or mitosis
S phase
Cytokinesis
questions.explain: DNA is replicated during S, the synthesis phase of interphase, so DNA content per cell doubles before mitosis distributes it.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the checkpoint that pauses the cycle when DNA is damaged?
choices: To speed cells through division regardless of damage
To permanently stop all cell division in the body
To convert the cell into a gamete
To allow time for repair before the damage is copied and passed on
questions.explain: Checkpoints halt the cycle so damage can be repaired before replication or division, preventing errors from being passed to daughter cells.

questions.stem: In the mutant line missing the damage checkpoint protein, what is the most likely outcome after DNA is damaged?
choices: The cells divide despite the damage, passing mutations to daughter cells
The cells repair perfectly and never divide again
The cells immediately die before dividing
The damage repairs itself without any checkpoint
questions.explain: Without the checkpoint to pause the cycle, damaged DNA is replicated and segregated, so daughter cells inherit mutations, a step toward cancer.

questions.stem: Progress through the cycle is driven by enzymes that are active only when bound to a partner protein whose level rises and falls at each stage. Which pair fits this description?
choices: DNA polymerase activated by RNA
Cyclin dependent kinases activated by cyclins
Ribosomes activated by tRNA
Hemoglobin activated by oxygen
questions.explain: Cyclin dependent kinases are active only when bound to cyclins, whose levels oscillate through the cycle, driving orderly progression.

questions.stem: A single fertilized egg gives rise to muscle cells and nerve cells that look and act very differently, yet all carry the same DNA. What best explains this difference?
choices: Each cell type deleted the genes it does not use
Muscle and nerve cells have completely different genomes
Different cell types express different subsets of the same genes
The egg divided its genome unequally among cell types
questions.explain: Differentiation results from differential gene expression, so cells with identical genomes turn on different sets of genes to become specialized types.

questions.stem: A cell with irreparable DNA damage triggers an orderly self destruction program rather than dividing. This programmed cell death is called...
choices: Necrosis from injury
Binary fission
Differentiation
Apoptosis
questions.explain: Apoptosis is programmed, controlled cell death that removes damaged or unneeded cells, unlike the messy injury driven death of necrosis.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A neurophysiology lab records electrical activity from a single neuron. At rest the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside, and this difference is maintained by ion pumps and channels. When the neuron is stimulated strongly enough, a rapid spike of voltage travels down the axon.

The team can block specific ion channels and can wrap or strip the axon's insulating sheath. They also study how a hormone released into the blood affects distant target cells, comparing a steroid hormone with a protein hormone.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 12 (The Nervous System and Nervous Tissue) and Ch. 17 (The Endocrine System)

questions.stem: At rest, the neuron's interior is negative compared with the outside. Which best accounts for maintaining this resting membrane potential?
choices: Active pumping of sodium out and potassium in, plus selective ion permeability
Equal, unregulated leak of all ions across the membrane
Continuous firing of action potentials
The absence of any ions inside the cell
questions.explain: The sodium potassium pump together with the membrane's selective permeability, especially to potassium, sets up and maintains the negative resting potential.

questions.stem: During the rising phase of the action potential, the membrane voltage rapidly becomes positive inside. Which ion movement is chiefly responsible?
choices: Potassium rushing into the cell
Sodium rushing into the cell
Chloride rushing out of the cell
Calcium leaving the cell
questions.explain: Voltage gated sodium channels open and sodium flows in down its gradient, driving the sharp depolarization of the action potential.

questions.stem: A weak stimulus produces no action potential, but once the stimulus reaches threshold the spike fires at full size, and a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger spike. This behavior is described as...
choices: A graded response proportional to stimulus size
A response that grows with stimulus strength without limit
An all or none response above threshold
A response that requires no threshold at all
questions.explain: Action potentials are all or none, so below threshold nothing fires and at or above threshold the spike reaches its full fixed amplitude regardless of extra stimulus strength.

questions.stem: When the team strips the insulating sheath from the axon, the action potential travels much more slowly. What does the intact sheath normally do?
choices: It generates the action potential at each point along the axon
It supplies ATP to the axon
It blocks all ion movement across the axon permanently
It lets the signal jump between gaps, speeding conduction
questions.explain: Myelin insulates the axon so the impulse regenerates only at the nodes between segments, jumping node to node in saltatory conduction and greatly speeding transmission.

questions.stem: A steroid hormone acts on its target cells more slowly but with longer lasting effects than a protein hormone. Which difference best explains this?
choices: Steroid hormones are lipid soluble, enter cells, and often alter gene transcription directly
Steroid hormones bind surface receptors and act through fast second messengers
Protein hormones enter the nucleus while steroids stay outside
Steroid hormones cannot reach target cells through the blood
questions.explain: Lipid soluble steroids cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription, a slower but longer lasting route than the surface receptor and second messenger pathway of peptide hormones.

questions.stem: When blood levels of a hormone rise, they signal the gland to reduce further release of that hormone. This regulatory pattern is...
choices: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward amplification
An all or none response
questions.explain: Negative feedback opposes the initial change, so rising hormone levels inhibit further secretion and keep levels within a set range.

passages.label: Case
paragraphs: A sports physiologist monitors a volunteer during hard exercise. Heart rate and breathing rate rise, the working muscles receive more blood, and the volunteer sweats heavily. The physiologist records oxygen delivery, carbon dioxide removal, and how the kidneys adjust urine output.
They also examine how oxygen is carried in the blood and how contracting muscle fibers shorten. All measurements are compared with the same volunteer at rest.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 20 (Cardiovascular System: Blood Vessels and Circulation), Ch. 22 (Respiratory System), and Ch. 25 (Urinary System)

questions.stem: During exercise the volunteer's heart rate and the volume pumped per beat both rise. The total blood pumped per minute, the product of these two, is called...
choices: Blood pressure
Vital capacity
Cardiac output
Tidal volume
questions.explain: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so raising both increases the blood delivered to tissues per minute during exercise.

questions.stem: Working muscle is warmer, more acidic, and higher in carbon dioxide than resting tissue. How does this environment affect oxygen release from hemoglobin there?
choices: It makes hemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly, releasing less
It has no effect on oxygen binding
It stops hemoglobin from binding oxygen in the lungs
It promotes oxygen release, so more oxygen is unloaded to active muscle
questions.explain: Higher carbon dioxide, lower pH, and higher temperature lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve so more oxygen is unloaded where active tissue needs it most.

questions.stem: Breathing rate rises sharply during exercise. What is the most direct benefit of increased ventilation for the working body?
choices: It brings in more oxygen and clears more carbon dioxide
It cools the blood by evaporation in the lungs
It raises blood pressure directly
It increases the number of red blood cells immediately
questions.explain: Greater ventilation increases oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal at the alveoli, matching the higher metabolic demand of exercise.

questions.stem: Because the volunteer loses a lot of water through sweat, the kidneys produce a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. This adjustment mainly helps to...
choices: Excrete excess glucose
Conserve body water and maintain blood volume
Remove extra oxygen from the blood
Increase sweating even further
questions.explain: Facing water loss, the kidneys reabsorb more water and produce concentrated urine to conserve body water and help maintain blood volume and pressure.

questions.stem: In contracting muscle fibers, the filaments slide past one another so the muscle shortens. Which statement best describes this process?
choices: Actin and myosin filaments each shorten individually
The filaments dissolve and reform shorter
Myosin heads pull actin filaments inward, shortening the sarcomere without shortening the filaments
Only myosin filaments move while actin stays fixed permanently
questions.explain: In the sliding filament model, myosin cross bridges pull actin toward the center of the sarcomere, so the filaments keep their length while the sarcomere shortens.

questions.stem: During hard exercise, blood flow to the digestive tract drops while flow to muscles rises. What is the most reasonable consequence?
choices: Digestion speeds up because muscles need nutrients
The stomach produces more blood cells
The intestines take over gas exchange
Digestion and absorption slow while more blood serves active muscle
questions.explain: Blood is redirected toward working muscle during exercise, so digestive activity slows because the gut temporarily receives less blood flow.

passages.label: Titration
paragraphs: A biochemistry lab titrates a dilute solution of the amino acid glycine, starting at very low pH and slowly adding a strong base while recording pH. At the start both ionizable groups are fully protonated, so the carboxyl group is neutral and the amino group carries a positive charge, giving the molecule a net charge of plus one. As base is added, the carboxyl group gives up its proton first, near a pKa of 2.3, leaving a species with no net charge called a zwitterion. Adding still more base eventually removes the proton from the amino group, near a pKa of 9.6, giving the molecule a net charge of minus one. The lab notes two regions where the pH changes slowly, one around each pKa, where the solution resists change.

The team repeats the titration with two other amino acids. Aspartate has a second carboxyl group on its side chain, adding a third ionizable group with a low pKa, while lysine has a second amino group on its side chain with a high pKa. For each amino acid they identify the pH at which the average net charge is exactly zero, called the isoelectric point. They observe that the extra acidic group on aspartate pulls its isoelectric point to a low pH, whereas the extra basic group on lysine raises its isoelectric point to a high pH. The class uses these curves to predict the charge each amino acid would carry in solutions of different pH.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (Acid-base chemistry of amino acids)

questions.stem: At the very start of the titration, at very low pH, what is the net charge on glycine?
choices: Net positive, plus one, because both the amino and carboxyl groups are protonated
Zero, because it exists as a neutral zwitterion
Net negative, minus one, because the carboxyl group has lost its proton
Net negative, minus two, because both groups are deprotonated
questions.explain: At a pH below both pKa values the carboxyl group stays protonated and neutral while the amino group holds its proton and its positive charge, giving a net charge of plus one. The zwitterion answer is wrong because that neutral form appears only at higher pH, once the carboxyl group has lost its proton.

questions.stem: As base is added to the glycine solution, which group gives up its proton first?
choices: The amino group, which has a pKa near 9.6
The carboxyl group, which has a pKa near 2.3
The alpha carbon, which has no pKa
The side chain of glycine, which is a single hydrogen
questions.explain: The group with the lower pKa loses its proton first, and the carboxyl group at pKa 2.3 ionizes well before the amino group at pKa 9.6. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen, so it has no ionizable group to lose.

questions.stem: The isoelectric point of an amino acid is best defined as which of the following?
choices: The pH at which the molecule is fully protonated
The pH at which the carboxyl group first begins to ionize
The pH at which the average net charge is zero
The pH at which the amino group is fully deprotonated
questions.explain: The isoelectric point is defined as the pH at which the molecule carries no average net charge. It is not the pH where a group begins to ionize or where the molecule is fully protonated.

questions.stem: Using its two pKa values of 2.3 and 9.6, the isoelectric point of glycine is approximately...
choices: About 2.3, the lower pKa
About 6.0, the average of the two pKa values
About 9.6, the higher pKa
About 11.9, the sum of the two pKa values
questions.explain: For an amino acid whose only charged groups are the alpha carboxyl and alpha amino, the isoelectric point is the average of the two pKa values, so 2.3 plus 9.6 divided by 2 is about 6.0. The individual pKa values themselves are not the point of zero net charge.

questions.stem: Near pH 2.3 the glycine solution resists changes in pH strongly. Why does it buffer well at that pH?
choices: It has no ionizable groups near that pH
Near that pH about half the carboxyl groups are protonated and half are not, so it resists pH change
It is fully positive there and cannot accept protons
Water alone does the buffering, not the amino acid
questions.explain: A weak acid buffers best when the pH is near its pKa, where roughly half the groups are protonated and half are not, so added acid or base is absorbed with little change in pH. At that pH the molecule can both donate and accept protons.

questions.stem: Aspartate carries an extra carboxyl group on its side chain compared with glycine. How does this affect its isoelectric point?
choices: Its isoelectric point is lower than glycine's, because the extra acidic group must stay protonated to reach zero net charge
Its isoelectric point is higher than glycine's, because the extra group is basic
Its isoelectric point is unchanged, because side chains never ionize
Aspartate has no isoelectric point at all
questions.explain: Aspartate has two acidic carboxyl groups, so reaching zero net charge requires a lower pH where the extra group stays protonated, pulling the isoelectric point below that of glycine. It is not raised, because the added group is acidic rather than basic.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A microbiology lab investigates how DNA is copied. They grow bacteria for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source is a heavy isotope, so every DNA strand becomes dense. They then move the cells to a medium with ordinary light nitrogen and allow exactly one round of division before extracting the DNA and spinning it to separate molecules by density. After this first round every DNA molecule is of a single intermediate density, halfway between fully heavy and fully light. The team lets a second set of cells divide once more and finds that the DNA now separates into two groups, half at intermediate density and half fully light. They use these bands to decide among competing models of replication.

Next the lab looks closely at a replication fork, the point where the double helix is opened and copied. DNA polymerase can add new nucleotides only to the growing three prime end of a strand, so it builds each new strand in the five prime to three prime direction. Because the two template strands run in opposite directions, one new strand is made continuously toward the moving fork, while the other is made in short pieces that point away from the fork and are joined together later. An enzyme called primase first lays down a short RNA primer to give the polymerase a starting point. The polymerase also checks its work, removing a mismatched nucleotide right after adding it, which keeps copying errors rare.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 14 (DNA Structure and Function)

questions.stem: After one round of division in light nitrogen, all the DNA is of a single intermediate density. This result supports which model of replication?
choices: A conservative pattern, with the original duplex left intact
A semiconservative pattern, with one old and one new strand per duplex
A dispersive pattern, with strands broken into many pieces
No copying of the template at all
questions.explain: A single intermediate band after one round means each new duplex contains one old heavy strand and one new light strand, which is the semiconservative pattern. A conservative model would leave the original heavy duplex intact and produce a separate fully light duplex, giving two bands rather than one.

questions.stem: After a second round of division in light nitrogen, what density pattern is expected?
choices: All heavy DNA
All intermediate density DNA
Half intermediate density and half fully light DNA
Equal amounts of fully heavy and fully light DNA
questions.explain: In the second round the original heavy strands pair with new light strands to give intermediate duplexes, while the strands made in the first round pair with new light strands to give fully light duplexes, so half is intermediate and half is light. All intermediate is the one round result, not the two round result.

questions.stem: DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to which part of the growing strand?
choices: The five prime end of the growing strand
The three prime end of the growing strand
The middle of the growing strand
Either end, chosen at random
questions.explain: DNA polymerase builds a strand only in the five prime to three prime direction, adding each new nucleotide to the free three prime end. It cannot add to the five prime end.

questions.stem: Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand is built in short pieces pointing away from the fork. These short pieces are characteristic of the...
choices: leading strand, which is made continuously
lagging strand, which is made in short pieces
RNA primer, which is made of protein
parental heavy strand
questions.explain: The strand made in short pieces away from the fork is the lagging strand, and those pieces are the Okazaki fragments. The leading strand is instead made continuously toward the fork.

questions.stem: What is the role of primase at the start of replication?
choices: It unwinds the double helix ahead of the fork
It seals the gaps between finished fragments
It lays down a short RNA primer that gives the polymerase a three prime end to extend
It proofreads and removes mismatched bases
questions.explain: Primase lays down a short RNA primer that provides the three prime end DNA polymerase needs to begin adding nucleotides. Unwinding the helix and sealing gaps are jobs of other enzymes.

questions.stem: A variant DNA polymerase lacks the proofreading activity that removes a wrongly paired base right after it is added. This variant would most likely show...
choices: a higher mutation rate in the DNA it copies
no change in accuracy at all
a complete inability to add any nucleotides
faster replication that is still perfectly accurate
questions.explain: Proofreading removes a mismatched base immediately, so a polymerase without it leaves more errors in place and raises the mutation rate. It would still add nucleotides, just less accurately.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A cell biology lab studies how a eukaryotic cell controls which of its genes are switched on. Inside the nucleus the long DNA molecule is wound around histone proteins and packed into a fiber called chromatin. Where the fiber is packed tightly, the machinery that reads genes cannot reach the DNA, so those genes stay quiet. Chemical tags can change the packing. Adding acetyl groups to the histones loosens the fiber and opens the DNA, while removing them tightens it again. Starting transcription of a gene also depends on regulatory proteins called transcription factors, which bind specific DNA sequences and help position the enzyme that copies the gene. The team can add drugs that block the tagging enzymes and can mutate the regulatory sequences a gene needs.

The lab also follows what happens to a gene's RNA after it is copied. The first transcript is processed before it can leave the nucleus. A protective cap is added to one end and a long tail of adenine nucleotides to the other, and stretches called introns that do not code for protein are cut out while the coding exons are joined together. By joining the exons in different combinations, one gene can give rise to more than one related protein. The team labels a transcript before and after this processing, measures how its length changes, and records how stable the finished message is once it reaches the cytoplasm to be translated.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 16 (Gene Expression)

questions.stem: Genes in a region of tightly packed chromatin tend to be transcriptionally...
choices: highly active, because tight packing recruits the machinery
generally silent, because the machinery cannot reach the DNA
unaffected, because packing does not matter for transcription
turned directly into protein without transcription
questions.explain: When chromatin is packed tightly the transcription machinery cannot reach the DNA, so those genes are generally silent. Packing does not recruit polymerase or turn DNA directly into protein.

questions.stem: Adding acetyl groups to histones loosens the chromatin fiber. What effect does this most likely have on nearby genes?
choices: It decreases their transcription by tightening the fiber
It has no effect on transcription
It increases their transcription by opening access to the DNA
It permanently deletes the genes
questions.explain: Histone acetylation loosens the fiber and exposes the DNA, which generally makes nearby genes easier to transcribe. It does not tighten the fiber or delete genes.

questions.stem: Cutting out introns and joining the coding exons of a transcript together is called...
choices: capping
splicing
replication
translation
questions.explain: Removing introns and joining the exons is called splicing. Capping instead adds a protective group to one end of the transcript.

questions.stem: By joining the exons of one gene in different combinations, a cell can make several related proteins. This process is called...
choices: alternative splicing
a point mutation
semiconservative replication
independent assortment
questions.explain: Joining the exons of one gene in different combinations to yield several proteins is alternative splicing. A point mutation changes a single base and does not by itself generate multiple protein forms from one transcript.

questions.stem: The cap and the adenine tail added during processing mainly help the messenger RNA to...
choices: be destroyed faster once it is made
be protected and to leave the nucleus and be translated
have its coding exons removed
copy the DNA template again
questions.explain: The cap and poly-A tail protect the messenger RNA from breakdown and help it leave the nucleus and be translated. They do not speed its destruction or remove exons.

questions.stem: Two cell types in the same organism carry identical DNA yet make different proteins, in part because different transcription factors are active in each. This is best explained by...
choices: each cell type carrying a different genome
each cell type turning on a different subset of the same genes
each cell type randomly losing chromosomes
each cell type having its own unique mutations
questions.explain: Cells with identical DNA differ because each turns on a different subset of the shared genes, controlled in part by which transcription factors are active. They do not carry different genomes or delete unused genes.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A genetics class studies meiosis, the special cell division that makes gametes such as eggs and sperm. A cell that is diploid carries two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Before meiosis the cell copies all of its DNA once. It then goes through two rounds of division without copying again, so the four cells produced are haploid and carry a single copy of each chromosome. In the first division the matching pairs of chromosomes, called homologs, line up together and are pulled to opposite ends of the cell. In the second division the two identical halves of each chromosome finally separate. The class watches how alleles from the two parents are shuffled during this process.

Two features of meiosis create new combinations of alleles. First, when homologs pair in the first division they can swap matching segments, a trade called crossing over that mixes parental alleles on a single chromosome. Second, each pair of homologs lines up independently of the other pairs, so maternal and paternal chromosomes are dealt into gametes in many combinations. The class also studies mistakes. If a pair of homologs or a pair of chromosome halves fails to separate, an event called nondisjunction, some gametes end up with an extra chromosome and others with one too few. When such a gamete joins a normal one at fertilization, the offspring carries an abnormal number of that chromosome.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 11 (Meiosis and Sexual Reproduction)

questions.stem: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number from diploid to haploid. Why is this reduction important?
choices: It doubles the chromosome number so gametes are diploid
It makes gametes haploid so that fertilization can restore the diploid number
It keeps gametes diploid, which they need to function
It removes all genetic variation from the gametes
questions.explain: Halving the chromosome number in gametes means that when two gametes fuse at fertilization the normal diploid number is restored. Without the reduction, the number would double every generation.

questions.stem: During which division do homologous chromosomes separate from each other?
choices: Meiosis I
Meiosis II
Mitosis
Fertilization
questions.explain: Homologous chromosomes pair and then separate during meiosis I, which is why it is called the reduction division. Sister chromatids stay together until meiosis II.

questions.stem: How does crossing over between homologous chromosomes increase genetic variation?
choices: By copying whole chromosomes for the gamete
By exchanging matching segments so chromatids carry new allele combinations
By removing alleles from the chromosome
By keeping homologs from ever separating
questions.explain: Crossing over physically exchanges matching segments between homologs, producing chromatids with new combinations of alleles. It does not copy whole chromosomes or remove alleles.

questions.stem: The random way each homolog pair orients at the metaphase plate, independently of the other pairs, is the cellular basis of...
choices: the independent assortment of genes on different chromosomes
the replication of DNA before division
nondisjunction of the chromosomes
the blending of parental traits
questions.explain: Each homolog pair orients randomly and independently at the metaphase plate, which is the cellular basis of the independent assortment of genes on different chromosomes. This is separate from nondisjunction, which is a failure of separation.

questions.stem: Nondisjunction is best defined as...
choices: the normal, orderly separation of chromosomes
the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate properly
the exchange of segments between homologs
the fusion of two gametes at fertilization
questions.explain: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiosis. It is not normal separation or the exchange of segments.

questions.stem: A gamete produced by nondisjunction carries an extra copy of one chromosome. If it is fertilized by a normal gamete, the offspring cell will have...
choices: the normal diploid number for every chromosome
three copies of that chromosome instead of the usual two
a single copy of every chromosome
no copies of that chromosome at all
questions.explain: The extra chromosome in the gamete plus the normal copy from the other gamete gives the offspring three copies of that chromosome instead of two. It does not produce a normal set or a missing chromosome in this case.

passages.label: Field study
paragraphs: Field biologists follow a large population of beetles whose body color is set by a single gene. A dark allele is dominant to a light allele. The beetles rest on dark tree bark, where hunting birds spot light colored beetles more easily and eat them, while dark beetles are better hidden and survive to reproduce more often. Over many seasons the team records the fraction of dark and light beetles and estimates how common each allele is in the population. They confirm that the population is large, that beetles mate without regard to color, and that few beetles enter or leave, so they can focus on how survival differences alone shift the alleles.

For comparison the team studies a very small population on a nearby island that was started by only a handful of beetles. By chance those few founders happened to carry mostly the light allele, so the island population looks different from the mainland one from the start. The researchers track how allele frequencies drift over the generations in this small group, where chance events have a large effect. They discuss the idealized conditions under which allele frequencies would not change at all, a baseline called Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and identify which real forces are pushing each population away from that baseline.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 19 (The Evolution of Populations)

questions.stem: Because birds eat light beetles more easily on dark bark, dark beetles leave more offspring. Over many generations the frequency of the dark allele will most likely...
choices: increase over the generations
decrease over the generations
stay exactly constant
disappear completely in a single generation
questions.explain: Because dark beetles survive and reproduce more on dark bark, they pass on more dark alleles, so that allele's frequency rises over generations. A dominant allele is not automatically more or less common, so decrease is wrong.

questions.stem: This change in allele frequency, driven by consistent differences in survival and reproduction, is an example of...
choices: genetic drift
natural selection
gene flow from another population
a directed mutation caused by the birds
questions.explain: A frequency change caused by consistent differences in survival and reproduction is natural selection. Genetic drift instead refers to change from random chance, not from a survival advantage.

questions.stem: In the small island population, allele frequencies shifted largely because a few chance founders were not representative of the source. This is best described as...
choices: natural selection favoring the light allele
genetic drift, specifically a founder effect
steady gene flow from the mainland
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
questions.explain: Allele frequencies in the small island group shifted because a few unrepresentative founders started it, a form of genetic drift called the founder effect. This is chance, not the selective advantage that defines natural selection.

questions.stem: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a population whose allele frequencies do not change. Which set of conditions must hold for it?
choices: Strong natural selection on the trait
Frequent nonrandom mating
No selection, drift, migration, or mutation, together with random mating
A very small population size
questions.explain: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium holds only when there is no selection, no drift, no migration, and no mutation, and mating is random. Strong selection or a small population would push frequencies away from equilibrium.

questions.stem: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium the dark allele frequency is 0.6 and the light allele frequency is 0.4. What fraction of beetles are homozygous for the light allele?
questions.explain: The frequency of the homozygous light genotype is q squared, and with q equal to 0.4 that is 0.16. The value 0.48 would be the heterozygote frequency, 2pq, not the homozygous recessive one.

questions.stem: Which process ultimately provides the new genetic variation that natural selection then acts on?
choices: Mutation
Homeostasis
Reshuffling of existing alleles with no new ones
The isoelectric point of the allele
questions.explain: New alleles ultimately arise from mutation, which supplies the raw variation that selection acts on. Independent assortment and recombination only rearrange alleles that already exist.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A biochemistry group measures the energy changes of reactions inside cells. They sort reactions into two kinds. An exergonic reaction releases free energy and has a negative change in Gibbs free energy, so it can move toward products on its own. An endergonic reaction absorbs free energy and has a positive change, so it does not move toward products by itself. The group notes that the breakdown of ATP into ADP and a free phosphate group is strongly exergonic, releasing a useful amount of energy. Cells rely on this reaction again and again as a way to supply energy where it is needed.

To build large molecules the cell links an uphill endergonic reaction to the downhill breakdown of ATP, so that the two reactions considered together release energy overall and can proceed. The group also points out that being exergonic does not guarantee a fast reaction. Many favorable reactions crawl along because they must first pass over a high energy barrier called the activation energy. Enzymes speed these reactions up by lowering that barrier, which lets far more reactant molecules react each second. Importantly, an enzyme does not change whether a reaction is favorable, only how quickly it reaches its result. The group measures each reaction with and without its enzyme present.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 6 (Metabolism)

questions.stem: A reaction that releases free energy and has a negative change in Gibbs free energy is called...
choices: endergonic
exergonic
nonspontaneous
at equilibrium
questions.explain: A reaction that releases free energy and has a negative change in Gibbs free energy is exergonic. Endergonic reactions are the opposite, absorbing energy with a positive change.

questions.stem: An endergonic reaction, considered by itself, will...
choices: proceed toward products on its own
not proceed toward products without an input of energy
always run extremely fast
release energy to the surroundings
questions.explain: An endergonic reaction has a positive free energy change, so on its own it will not move toward products without an added energy source. It does not release energy or run quickly by itself.

questions.stem: How does the cell drive an endergonic reaction such as building a macromolecule?
choices: By coupling it to the exergonic breakdown of ATP
By lowering the temperature of the cell
By removing all enzymes from the cell
By waiting for it to happen on its own
questions.explain: The cell pairs the uphill endergonic reaction with the strongly exergonic breakdown of ATP so the combined process is favorable. Lowering temperature or removing enzymes would not make an endergonic reaction proceed.

questions.stem: Two coupled reactions will proceed only if...
choices: each reaction on its own has a positive free energy change
the sum of their free energy changes is negative overall
the activation energy of the pair is raised
the ATP is changed into a form that cannot be broken down
questions.explain: Two coupled reactions will proceed only if the sum of their free energy changes is negative, even if one of them is positive on its own. If each stayed positive, the pair would still not go.

questions.stem: A reaction is strongly exergonic yet proceeds extremely slowly on its own. What is the most likely reason?
choices: It is actually endergonic despite appearances
It faces a high activation energy barrier
It releases no free energy
It is already sitting at equilibrium
questions.explain: A favorable reaction can still be very slow if it faces a high activation energy barrier that few molecules can cross each second. Being slow does not make it endergonic or mean it releases no energy.

questions.stem: An enzyme speeds this reaction up by...
choices: making the reaction more exergonic
lowering the free energy of the products
lowering the activation energy without changing whether the reaction is favorable
supplying the free energy the reaction lacks
questions.explain: An enzyme speeds a reaction by lowering its activation energy, letting more molecules react each second, without changing whether the reaction is favorable. It does not make the reaction more exergonic or supply energy to it.

passages.label: Case
paragraphs: A metabolism lab tracks how the body fuels itself between meals. Soon after a meal rich in carbohydrate, the level of glucose in the blood is high. Cells take up glucose and burn some of it right away for energy, and the body tucks away the extra. The liver and muscles store surplus glucose by linking the molecules into a branched polymer called glycogen, while fat is stored in adipose tissue. The lab samples blood glucose, measures glycogen stores in liver and muscle, and follows the level of small acidic molecules called ketone bodies, comparing values during feeding and during a long fast.

As a fast goes on, blood glucose starts to fall, so the liver breaks its stored glycogen back down into glucose and releases it to the blood. When glycogen stores run low after a longer fast, the body leans more on stored fat, sending fatty acids to tissues that oxidize them for energy. The liver turns some of the products of fat breakdown into ketone bodies, a fuel the brain can use when glucose is scarce. The body can even build new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as certain amino acids. The lab records which fuel supplies most of the energy at each stage of the fast.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 7 (Cellular Respiration)

questions.stem: Right after a carbohydrate meal, excess glucose is stored in the liver and muscle mainly as...
choices: glycogen
extra protein in the blood
ketone bodies in the liver
DNA in the nucleus
questions.explain: Surplus glucose after a meal is stored in the liver and muscle as glycogen, a branched polymer of glucose. It is not stored as protein or as ketone bodies.

questions.stem: During early fasting, blood glucose is kept up mainly by the liver...
choices: making new fat from glucose
breaking stored glycogen back down into glucose
storing even more glucose as glycogen
making ketone bodies out of glucose
questions.explain: In early fasting the liver breaks stored glycogen back into glucose and releases it to keep blood glucose up. Storing more glycogen would lower blood glucose, the opposite of what is needed.

questions.stem: After a longer fast, once glycogen stores are low, which fuel does the body increasingly rely on?
choices: Stored fat, whose fatty acids are oxidized for energy
A fresh supply of dietary carbohydrate
Nucleic acids taken from the diet
Oxygen stored in the muscles
questions.explain: Once glycogen runs low, the body increasingly oxidizes fatty acids from stored fat for energy. There is no incoming dietary carbohydrate during a fast, so that option does not apply.

questions.stem: The liver makes ketone bodies from the products of fat breakdown during a prolonged fast. A key benefit is that ketone bodies...
choices: give the brain a usable fuel when glucose is scarce
are stored away as glycogen
take the place of oxygen in respiration
cannot be used by any tissue
questions.explain: Ketone bodies made by the liver from fat breakdown give the brain a usable fuel when glucose is scarce. They are not stored as glycogen and are certainly usable, so those options are wrong.

questions.stem: During an extended fast the body can make new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as certain amino acids. This process is called...
choices: glycolysis
gluconeogenesis
fermentation
glycogen synthesis
questions.explain: Making new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as amino acids is gluconeogenesis. Glycolysis instead breaks glucose down, and glycogen synthesis stores it.

questions.stem: Fatty acids, glucose, and amino acids can all be broken down into intermediates that feed the same central pathways. This shows that the body's metabolic pathways are...
choices: completely separate, sharing no steps
interconnected, feeding into shared pathways such as the citric acid cycle
unable to use fat as an energy source
active only right after a meal
questions.explain: Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are broken down into intermediates that feed shared pathways such as the citric acid cycle, showing that metabolism is interconnected. The pathways are not separate, and fat certainly can be used for energy.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A signaling lab studies how a water soluble hormone changes a cell without ever entering it. Because the hormone cannot cross the greasy interior of the membrane, it binds to a receptor protein that spans the membrane. When the hormone attaches to the outside part of the receptor, the receptor changes shape on the inside, and this switches on an enzyme at the inner surface. The enzyme makes many copies of a small molecule that spreads through the cytoplasm, known as a second messenger. The second messenger then switches on other enzymes deeper in the cell, so a message received at the surface is passed inward. The lab can measure hormone binding, second messenger levels, and the cell's final response.

The team notices that a tiny amount of hormone produces a large effect. Each receptor that is switched on can activate many enzyme molecules, and each of those can make many second messenger molecules, so the signal grows at every step in a cascade. This amplification lets a few hormone molecules change the behavior of a whole cell. For contrast, the lab also studies a steroid signal, which is lipid soluble and slips straight through the membrane to bind a receptor inside the cell. That internal receptor often acts on the genes, and the team compares how quickly each pathway acts and how long each effect lasts.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 9 (Cell Communication)

questions.stem: A water soluble hormone cannot cross the plasma membrane. To affect the cell it must...
choices: bind a receptor on the outside of the cell surface
diffuse freely through the lipid interior of the membrane
be turned into a gas to slip inside
enter straight through the nucleus
questions.explain: A water soluble hormone cannot pass through the lipid interior of the membrane, so it must bind a receptor on the cell surface to act. It cannot diffuse freely through the bilayer the way a lipid soluble signal can.

questions.stem: The small molecule made inside the cell that relays the signal from the receptor is called a...
choices: first messenger
second messenger
signaling ligand
substrate that the hormone breaks down
questions.explain: The small molecule made inside the cell that relays the signal from the receptor is a second messenger. The hormone itself is the first messenger, not the second.

questions.stem: One hormone molecule triggers a very large cellular response. This is best explained by...
choices: amplification through a cascade of activated enzymes
the hormone being used up very slowly
the receptor shutting down all downstream steps
the hormone entering the nucleus to act
questions.explain: Because each receptor activates many enzymes and each enzyme makes many second messenger molecules, the signal is amplified into a large response from a small trigger. The response is not caused by the hormone entering the nucleus, which it cannot do.

questions.stem: A steroid signal is lipid soluble and crosses the membrane to bind an intracellular receptor that often acts on genes. Compared with the surface receptor pathway, its effects are typically...
choices: faster to appear and shorter lived
slower to appear but longer lasting
identical in timing to the surface pathway
unable to change the cell in any way
questions.explain: A lipid soluble steroid enters the cell and often acts on genes, which takes longer to show but produces effects that last. The fast, short lived responses are more typical of the surface receptor and second messenger route.

questions.stem: In this pathway, the hormone that binds the receptor is acting as the...
choices: enzyme that makes the second messenger
signaling ligand that the receptor detects
second messenger itself
DNA template inside the nucleus
questions.explain: The hormone is the signaling ligand that the receptor detects, not the enzyme or the second messenger it triggers. The enzyme and second messenger act downstream of the hormone.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that makes the second messenger. In cells treated with the water soluble hormone, the most likely effect is that...
choices: the surface signal is still received but the downstream response is blunted
the response becomes even larger than before
the hormone can no longer bind its receptor at all
only the steroid pathway is affected
questions.explain: Blocking the enzyme that makes the second messenger leaves the surface receptor able to bind hormone but cuts off the internal relay, so the downstream response is blunted. It does not stop the hormone from binding its receptor.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A virology lab studies a retrovirus, a virus whose genome is made of single stranded RNA rather than DNA. When the virus infects a host cell, it brings along its own enzyme, called reverse transcriptase, which copies the RNA genome into a matching strand of DNA. This DNA version of the viral genome then slips into one of the host cell's own chromosomes. Sitting inside the host genome, the viral genes are copied and read by the host's ordinary machinery, which unknowingly makes fresh viral RNA and viral proteins. The virus is enveloped, wrapping itself in a piece of the host's own membrane as it buds off to leave the cell.

The lab tests several drugs, each aimed at a different step. One blocks reverse transcriptase, one blocks the enzyme that splices the viral DNA into the host chromosome, and one blocks the assembly of new virus particles. The team also finds that reverse transcriptase does not proofread its work, so the virus makes many copying mistakes and its genome changes quickly from one generation to the next. This rapid change helps the virus slip past the immune system and develop resistance to drugs. The team measures viral DNA, the amount of integrated virus, and the release of new particles under each treatment.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Microbiology (Viruses)

questions.stem: A retrovirus stores its genetic information as...
choices: double stranded DNA
single stranded RNA
a chain of protein
a ring of lipid
questions.explain: A retrovirus carries its genome as single stranded RNA, which its own enzyme later copies into DNA. It is not stored as DNA or protein in the incoming particle.

questions.stem: Reverse transcriptase carried by the virus catalyzes which unusual step?
choices: Copying DNA into RNA
Copying RNA into DNA
Copying protein into RNA
Turning glucose into ATP
questions.explain: Reverse transcriptase copies the viral RNA genome into DNA, the reverse of the usual DNA to RNA flow. It does not translate RNA into protein.

questions.stem: After the viral DNA is made, it inserts into the host chromosome. This integrated viral DNA is called a...
choices: provirus
capsid
plasmid
ribosome
questions.explain: Viral DNA that has inserted into the host chromosome is called a provirus. A capsid is the protein shell and a plasmid is a bacterial DNA circle, neither of which fits.

questions.stem: A drug that blocks reverse transcriptase would most directly prevent the virus from...
choices: binding to the surface of the host cell
budding out through the membrane
making a DNA copy of its RNA genome
translating the host cell's own proteins
questions.explain: Blocking reverse transcriptase stops the virus from making the DNA copy of its RNA genome, so integration cannot follow. It does not act on binding or budding, which are separate steps.

questions.stem: Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, so the virus mutates rapidly. A direct consequence is that...
choices: it evolves quickly, which helps it escape the immune system and resist drugs
it becomes unable to change its surface proteins
it stops replicating altogether
it makes the host permanently immune
questions.explain: Without proofreading the virus accumulates mutations quickly, so it can change its surface and escape the immune system and drug pressure. Rapid mutation is the opposite of being unable to change.

questions.stem: The virus is described as enveloped, meaning it is surrounded by...
choices: a rigid cell wall the virus builds for itself
a second nucleus taken from the host
a membrane taken from the host cell
a wrapping of host DNA
questions.explain: An enveloped virus is wrapped in a membrane it takes from the host cell as it buds out. It does not build a rigid wall of its own or wrap itself in host DNA.

passages.label: Case
paragraphs: A hematology lab studies where the many kinds of blood cells come from. Deep in the bone marrow sits an unspecialized cell called a hematopoietic stem cell. It has two important abilities. It can divide to make more copies of itself, and it can give rise to cells that mature into the specialized cells of the blood. Its descendants become red blood cells that carry oxygen, several kinds of white blood cells that fight infection, and the cell fragments called platelets that help blood clot. Chemical signals in the marrow steer each young cell down one path or another. The lab traces how a single kind of stem cell can supply this whole range of mature cells.

The team watches what happens as a young cell commits to one fate. A cell heading toward becoming a red blood cell switches on the genes for hemoglobin and gradually loses the option of becoming any other type, even though it still holds the same complete set of genes as every other body cell. A finished human red blood cell even pushes out its nucleus and can no longer divide. The lab compares the dividing stem cells with the fully specialized cells they produce, recording which genes each one switches on and whether each is still able to divide. By lining these stages up, the team builds a picture of how one cell type becomes many.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 18 (The Cardiovascular System: Blood)

questions.stem: A hematopoietic stem cell is described as unspecialized. Which two abilities define such a stem cell?
choices: It can only divide once and then die
It can renew itself and also give rise to specialized cell types
It carries a different genome from other body cells
It works only as a finished red blood cell
