questions.explain: A stem cell is defined by being able to renew itself and to give rise to specialized cell types. Carrying a different genome or being a mature red blood cell would contradict what a stem cell is.

questions.stem: Red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets all arise from one kind of stem cell. This shows that a single stem cell type can...
choices: produce only one kind of cell
give rise to several specialized cell types
change the genome of each descendant
avoid dividing altogether
questions.explain: That one stem cell type gives rise to red cells, white cells, and platelets shows a single stem cell can produce multiple specialized cell types. It clearly does not make only one kind of cell.

questions.stem: As a precursor commits to becoming a red blood cell, it switches on hemoglobin genes and can no longer become a white blood cell. This growing commitment to a specialized fate is called...
choices: replication of the cell's DNA
fertilization of the cell
differentiation toward a specialized fate
diffusion across the membrane
questions.explain: The growing commitment of a cell to a particular specialized fate is differentiation. Replication and fertilization are entirely different processes.

questions.stem: A red blood cell and a white blood cell from the same person carry the same genome yet look and act very differently. The best explanation is that they...
choices: contain entirely different DNA
came originally from different people
each deleted the genes they do not use
express different subsets of the same shared genes
questions.explain: Two cell types with the same genome differ because each expresses a different subset of the shared genes. They do not contain different DNA or come from different people.

questions.stem: A mature human red blood cell loses its nucleus and can no longer divide. Compared with the stem cell it came from, the mature cell is...
choices: less specialized and able to divide freely
more specialized but no longer able to divide
identical in every way to the stem cell
able to turn into any other cell type
questions.explain: The mature red blood cell is more specialized than its stem cell and, having lost its nucleus, can no longer divide. It is not less specialized or able to become any other cell type.

questions.stem: The bone marrow must keep producing blood cells throughout life. This continuous supply depends on the stem cell's ability to...
choices: divide by mitosis to renew itself while also making cells that specialize
undergo meiosis to produce gametes
stop dividing permanently once formed
fuse with mature red blood cells
questions.explain: Continuous blood production depends on the stem cell dividing by mitosis to both renew itself and generate cells that specialize. Meiosis makes gametes, not blood cells, so it does not apply here.

passages.label: Experiment
paragraphs: A neuroscience lab records how a signal passes from one neuron to the next across a chemical synapse, the narrow gap between them. When an action potential sweeps down the first neuron and reaches the end of its axon, it causes gated channels there to open and let calcium ions flow into the terminal. The rush of calcium makes small sacs called vesicles, which are filled with a chemical messenger, fuse with the membrane and dump that messenger into the gap. The messenger drifts across and binds receptors on the second neuron, where it changes the flow of ions and shifts that neuron's membrane voltage. The lab can measure both the release of messenger and the response it produces.

To probe the synapse the team runs several tests. They can block the calcium channels at the terminal, add a drug that stops the enzyme that normally clears the messenger from the gap, and apply molecules that force ion channels on the receiving cell to open or close. They find that some messengers push the receiving neuron toward firing by making its inside less negative, while others push it away from firing by making its inside more negative. Each result ties a specific step at the synapse to the response recorded in the second neuron, so the lab can map how a signal is passed on, strengthened, or silenced at the junction between two neurons.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 12 (The Nervous System and Nervous Tissue)

questions.stem: At a chemical synapse, the signal is carried from one neuron to the next across the gap by...
choices: a direct electrical arc across the gap
neurotransmitter molecules released into the gap
whole vesicles that cross the gap intact
the first axon physically touching the second neuron
questions.explain: At a chemical synapse the signal crosses the gap as neurotransmitter molecules released by the first neuron. There is no direct electrical arc, and the vesicles stay behind rather than crossing intact.

questions.stem: When the action potential reaches the axon terminal, the immediate trigger for neurotransmitter release is the influx of...
choices: calcium ions entering through voltage gated channels
potassium ions leaving the terminal
glucose molecules entering the terminal
large proteins crossing the membrane
questions.explain: The action potential opens voltage gated calcium channels at the terminal, and the calcium that flows in triggers vesicles to release their neurotransmitter. Potassium leaving the cell does not drive release.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the enzyme that normally clears the neurotransmitter from the synaptic gap. The most likely effect is that the neurotransmitter...
choices: is cleared from the gap faster than usual
can no longer bind its receptor
lingers in the gap and prolongs its effect on the receiving neuron
is turned into calcium
questions.explain: Blocking the enzyme that clears the neurotransmitter lets it stay in the gap longer and keep acting on the receiving neuron, which prolongs rather than shortens its effect.

questions.stem: A neurotransmitter that depolarizes the receiving neuron makes that neuron...
choices: more likely to reach threshold and fire
less likely to fire an action potential
permanently unable to fire again
locked in a hyperpolarized state
questions.explain: A neurotransmitter that depolarizes the receiving neuron brings it closer to threshold, making it more likely to fire. Depolarization is excitatory, not inhibitory.

questions.stem: Blocking the voltage gated calcium channels at the axon terminal would most directly...
choices: increase neurotransmitter release
prevent neurotransmitter release
speed the action potential along the axon
hyperpolarize the terminal by letting potassium in
questions.explain: Since calcium influx triggers vesicle release, blocking the calcium channels prevents the neuron from releasing its neurotransmitter. It would not increase release or speed the axon's own action potential.

questions.stem: Some neurotransmitters hyperpolarize the receiving cell, making its inside more negative. Their overall effect on that neuron is...
choices: excitatory, pushing the neuron to fire
inhibitory, lowering the chance the neuron fires
a guaranteed trigger of an action potential
a release of calcium into the gap
questions.explain: A neurotransmitter that hyperpolarizes the receiving cell moves it further from threshold, reducing the chance it fires, which is an inhibitory effect. That is the opposite of promoting firing.

passages.label: Case
paragraphs: A renal physiology lab studies how the kidney turns blood into urine. Blood first reaches a tiny ball of capillaries called the glomerulus, where the pressure of the blood pushes fluid through a filter. Water and small dissolved substances such as glucose, salts, and the waste urea pass through into the start of a long tubule, while blood cells and large proteins are held back and stay in the blood. The fluid that enters the tubule is called the filtrate. As the filtrate flows along the tubule, the body reclaims the substances it wants to keep and adds a few extra wastes, shaping the final urine.

The lab measures how the tubule changes the filtrate. Under normal conditions the tubule reabsorbs essentially all of the filtered glucose back into the blood, so almost no glucose is left in the urine. The team also studies how the body controls water loss. When a person is dehydrated, a hormone is released that makes part of the tubule more permeable to water, so more water is pulled back into the blood and the kidney puts out a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. The lab compares urine volume and content in well hydrated and dehydrated states, and after a substance blocks glucose reabsorption in the tubule.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Ch. 25 (The Urinary System)

questions.stem: At the glomerulus, blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood while water and small solutes enter the tubule. This step is best described as...
choices: filtration driven by blood pressure
active secretion of proteins into the tubule
reabsorption of blood cells
synthesis of new blood in the tubule
questions.explain: Pushing fluid and small solutes out of the blood at the glomerulus while holding back cells and large proteins is filtration driven by blood pressure. It is not secretion or reabsorption, which happen later along the tubule.

questions.stem: Useful substances in the filtrate, such as glucose and much of the water, are returned to the blood along the tubule. This process is called...
choices: filtration
reabsorption
secretion
excretion of large proteins
questions.explain: Returning useful filtered substances such as glucose and water from the tubule back to the blood is reabsorption. Filtration is the earlier step that put them into the tubule.

questions.stem: In a healthy person the tubule reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose. Therefore normal urine contains...
choices: almost no glucose
more glucose than the blood holds
nothing but glucose
no water at all
questions.explain: Because the tubule normally reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose, healthy urine contains almost none. Urine cannot end up with more glucose than the blood it came from.

questions.stem: In uncontrolled diabetes, blood glucose is so high that the filtered glucose exceeds the tubule's reabsorption capacity. The most likely result is that...
choices: no glucose is filtered in the first place
glucose spills over and appears in the urine
the kidney stops making urine entirely
all of the glucose is still reabsorbed
questions.explain: When filtered glucose exceeds the tubule's reabsorption capacity, the excess is left behind and glucose appears in the urine. Glucose is still filtered, and the kidney keeps making urine.

questions.stem: When the body is dehydrated, a hormone makes part of the tubule more permeable to water. The expected result is...
choices: a large volume of dilute urine
a smaller volume of more concentrated urine
no change in the urine at all
the loss of essentially all body water
questions.explain: The hormone released in dehydration makes the tubule more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and a smaller volume of concentrated urine forms. A large volume of dilute urine would be the opposite response.

questions.stem: A few wastes are moved from the blood into the tubule to be eliminated, rather than being filtered at the glomerulus. This active movement into the tubule is called...
choices: reabsorption back into the blood
filtration at the glomerulus
tubular secretion into the tubule
simple diffusion into the blood
questions.explain: Actively moving wastes from the blood into the tubule for removal is tubular secretion. Reabsorption moves substances the other way, from tubule back to blood.

passages.label: Designing an enzyme-inhibitor assay
paragraphs: A biochemistry lab studies a candidate drug that appears to slow an enzyme. The drug is dissolved in a small volume of alcohol and added to a tube holding the enzyme and its substrate, and that tube runs more slowly than an untreated tube.
Before publishing, the team designs follow-up experiments to be sure the slowdown is really caused by the drug and to work out how the drug acts.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Biology 2e, Ch. 1 (The Study of Life) and Ch. 6 (Metabolism)

questions.stem: The drug is dissolved in alcohol before it is added. To be sure any drop in activity is caused by the drug and not the alcohol, the best control tube contains:
choices: the enzyme and substrate with the same amount of alcohol but no drug
twice as much enzyme
no enzyme and no substrate
the drug but no enzyme
questions.explain: A solvent control receives the same solvent but not the active substance, so any effect can be traced to the inhibitor rather than to the solvent it was dissolved in.

questions.stem: To work out whether the drug is a competitive or a noncompetitive inhibitor, the most informative experiment measures the reaction rate:
choices: at a single substrate concentration
across a range of substrate concentrations, with and without the drug
with no substrate present
only at the highest possible temperature
questions.explain: A competitive inhibitor can be overcome by a large excess of substrate while a noncompetitive inhibitor cannot, so varying the substrate concentration with and without the inhibitor distinguishes the two.

questions.stem: In one run the tube with the drug was kept several degrees colder than the untreated tube. Why does this weaken the conclusion that the drug slowed the enzyme?
choices: Temperature has no effect on enzymes
Temperature also changes enzyme activity, so it is a confound that could explain the difference on its own
Colder tubes always speed enzymes up
The substrate would freeze solid
questions.explain: Because temperature is itself a variable that changes reaction and enzyme rates, a colder inhibitor tube adds a confounding variable, so the difference in activity cannot be assigned to the inhibitor unless temperature is kept the same.
